Submission received: 25 November 2024 / Revised: 2 January 2025 / Accepted: 15 January 2025 / Published: 16 January 2025 Abstract This paper aims to comprehensively explore the performance and influencing factors of the constructed wetland–microbial fuel cell (CW-MFC) system when treating brine with different concentrations. The main objective is to determine how different salinity levels affect the operation and treatment efficiency of the CW-MFC system. The research results show that Bruguiera gymnorrhiza exhibits strong salt tolerance and can be used as a wetland plant for the CW-MFC system. The closed-circuit CW-MFC system with planted plants has the best performance, with a chemical oxygen demand (COD) removal rate of 84.8%, a total nitrogen (TN) removal rate of 68.12%, and a chloride ion (Cl−) removal rate of 29.96%. The maximum power density is 64.79% higher than that of the system without planted plants. The power generation performance of the system first increases and then decreases with the increase in salinity, while the internal resistance keeps decreasing. When the salinity is 2%, the power generation effect is the best, with an average output voltage of 617.3 ± 25.7 mV and a power density of 45.83 mW/m2. The removal rates of COD and TN are inhibited with the increase in salinity, while the removal rate of total phosphorus (TP) is not significantly affected. The microbial community grows well under salt stress, but its structure is different. When the salinity is 1%, the optimal distance between electrodes is 10 cm. Considering the pollutant removal performance, the optimal hydraulic retention time is 3 days, and considering the power generation performance, the optimal hydraulic retention time is 2 days. This research provides important value for improving the performance of the CW-MFC system in treating brine. 1. Introduction With the increasingly severe problem of water shortage, seawater desalination, as an important open-source and increment technology of water resources, has received extensive attention [1,2]. Among them, reverse osmosis seawater desalination (SWRO) has been widely used around the world due to its numerous advantages [3]. China’s reverse osmosis seawater desalination technology has also achieved great development, and the relevant project scale has been continuously expanding. However, a large amount of concentrated brine will inevitably be produced during the seawater desalination process. Factors such as its salinity, temperature, and pollutants contained therein pose many hazards to the marine ecological environment, such as affecting the growth and reproduction of marine organisms and leading to the eutrophication of water bodies. Therefore, the treatment of concentrated brine has become a key issue that urgently needs to be resolved [4]. Currently, common concentrated brine treatment technologies after seawater desalination are divided into two types: environmentally friendly and traditional, but each has certain limitations. For example, salt-making and membrane separation technologies have high costs and are prone to clogging, and traditional methods such as discharge and deep-well injection have a great impact on the environment or are costly [5,6]. Therefore, it is urgent to seek better treatment technologies. Microbial fuel cells can recycle wastewater resources and achieve energy recovery [7]. There have already been studies on its application in the field of seawater desalination [8]. Constructed wetland (CW) technology has the advantages of low operating cost and being eco-friendly, and it plays an important role in the treatment of various types of wastewater [9,10]. The MFC device consists of an anode (anaerobic) region and a cathode (aerobic) region, which is highly compatible with the structure and function of the vertical up-flow CW system [11]. The microbial community composition and their relative abundance in CW-MFC have shown a drift from conventional CW with 4.5-fold enhanced COD removal kinetics [12]. Abou-elela, S. K [15] also reached the same conclusion. fetched_contents.text: Shifts in Microbial Community Structure and Co-occurrence Network along a Wide Soil Salinity Gradient Abstract The response of microbiomes to salinity has been clarified in different geographic scales or ecosystems. However, how soil microbial community structure and interaction respond to salinity across wide salinity range and climatic region is still unclearly resolved. To address this issue, we examined the microbial community’s composition in saline soils from two climatic regions (coastal wetland and arid desert). Our research confirms that soil salinity had a negative effect on soil nutrient content. Salinity decreased the relative abundance of bacteria, but increased archaea abundance, leading to the shifts from bacteria dominant community to archaea dominant community. Low-water medium-salinity soil (LWMS) had the most complex archaeal community network, whereas for bacteria, the most complex bacterial community network was observed in low-water high-salinity soils (LWHS). Key microbial taxa differed in three salinity gradients. Salinity, soil water content, pH, total nitrogen (TN), and soil organic carbon (SOC) were the main driving factors for the composition of archaeal and bacterial community. Salinity directly affected archaeal community, but indirectly influenced bacteria community through SOC; pH affected archaeal community indirectly through TN, but directly affected bacterial community. Our study suggests that soil salinity dramatically influences diversity, composition, and interactions within the microbial community. Keywords: salinization, community composition, key species, soil remediation 1. Introduction Soil salinization is a widespread issue. More than 900 million hectares of soil worldwide have been identified as being at risk of salinization driven by natural or anthropogenic processes [1]. Furthermore, the area of saline-alkaline land is increasing by approximately 1–1.5 million hectares annually [2]. Soil salinization is a detrimental process that causes the loss of topsoil and nutrient depletion due to the reduction in soil structure and decreased vegetation cover [3], low soil fertility, poor structure, and an imbalance between input and output [4]. Microbiomes play a crucial role in maintaining soil ecosystem quality, function and health [5,6]. They improve soil structure and aggregation by producing substances such as glues and polysaccharides that bind soil particles together. They also play a key role in nutrient cycling processes such as nitrogen fixation, nutrient mineralization, organic matter decomposition, and soil fertility [7]. Plenty of researches have demonstrated the effects of soil salinization on soil microbial community at different geographic scales, salinization stages, and in various ecosystems, including farmland [8,9], salt lake sediments [10,11,12], wetlands [13,14,15], and deserts [16,17,18], these evidences lead to the conclusion that soil salinization leads to a decrease in microbial diversity and alterations to the structure of microbial community [19], which is probably due to a filtering effect that favors salt-tolerant or halophilic microorganisms over salt-sensitive taxa [20]. However, many of the studies were conducted on specific ecosystems or in limited salinity ranges. Broad-scale investigation of microbial community composition, function and driving factors across different climatic, geographic and salinity ranges is still inadequate. Yang et al. carried out a survey in surface sediments of the Qinghai-Tibetan Lakes which provided insights into the composition of bacteria and archaea changes with salinity from saline to hypersaline (salinity from 0.6 to 324 g·L−1) [10]. Liang et al. investigated the biogeographical patterns of bacterial communities in saline soils of northeast China at a large salinity range (8.9 mS/cm to 352 mS/cm), but this research focused on bacteria, rather than Archaea [20]. Archaea are a distinct group of organisms with unique genetic, biochemical and physiological characteristics that thrive in extreme environments [21]. They exhibit a wide range of metabolic diversity, including methanogenesis [22] and biogeochemical cycles, such as nitrogen cycling [23,24]. Therefore, a comprehensive investigation encompassing a wide range of salinity and a broad-geographic scale, which includes both bacteria and archaea, is essential to deepen our understanding of the impact of salinity on microbiomes composition, function, and ecosystem management. In the soil community, most microorganisms may interact with each other to establish diverse relationships, including mutualism, commensalism, synergism, competition, parasitism, and predation. These relationships shape the structure and function of microbial communities [25]. Co-occurrence network analysis provides a powerful tool for exploring the complexity of microbial communities, revealing hidden relationships which are more difficult to analyze using traditional analytical approaches, and helping identify keystone taxa that play crucial roles in maintaining community structure and function. These taxa may have a disproportionate impact on the overall ecosystem dynamics and could be important targets for conservation or manipulation in microbial communities [25,26,27]. Clarification of the microbial community’s network characteristics and its response to salinity are important to advance our understanding of the ecological principles governing microbial interactions and screen keystone species. # How salinity affects microbial activity and community structure in MFCs

Salinity exerts a strong selective pressure on microbial communities in microbial fuel cells (MFCs), shifting which groups are sensitive, enriched, and structurally dominant across low, moderate, and high salinity. The evidence points to a general pattern: salt-tolerant or halophilic microbes gain prominence, while salt-sensitive taxa decline, and community composition changes in ways that can include shifts in archaeal and bacterial dominance, altered relative abundances, and changes in functional interactions [N3-F2][N4-R3][N6-R4].

## Which microbial groups are sensitive or enriched at different salinities

The strongest direct evidence is that halophilic and halotolerant microbes are specifically selected under saline conditions. The literature explicitly states that halophilic bacteria “have evolved strategies to survive in high saline concentrations” and that halotolerant and halophilic microorganisms “possess specific salt tolerance mechanisms” that make them promising in high-salt environments [N1-R1][N1-R2]. This is consistent with the broader idea that saline stress filters communities to favor salt-tolerant or halophilic taxa over salt-sensitive ones [N3-F2].

The evidence also shows that microbial community dynamics can change sharply with salinity. A study examining three salinity levels (3.5, 7, and 15 g/L NaCl) found that current production, organic removal rates, and bacterial community dynamics were all affected, indicating that microbial activity is not only reduced or enhanced depending on salinity but also reorganized [N4-R3]. Another broader microbial ecology study reports that soil salinity can dramatically alter diversity, composition, and interactions within microbial communities, with archaea becoming relatively more abundant while bacterial abundance may decrease, and that some key microbial taxa differ across salinity gradients [N3-F2]. Although this is not an MFC study, it provides a useful conceptual framework for interpreting MFC community shifts.

## How salinity alters electron transfer and metabolic pathways

The evidence is somewhat indirect, but it is clear that salinity changes microbial physiology in ways that affect electron transfer. The search material emphasizes that halophilic bacteria are remarkable for their ability to survive high salinity and that salt-tolerant microbes can have promising bioactivity under high-salt conditions [N1-R1][N1-R2]. In MFCs, this implies that electron transfer may be supported by taxa with salt-adapted metabolic pathways, rather than by generalist microbes that are inhibited at higher salinities.

The microbial ecology study also suggests that salinity can alter microbial interactions, including shifts in co-occurrence networks and keystone taxa, which can indirectly affect electron transfer by changing the functional connectivity of the community [N3-F2]. It also notes that salinity can indirectly influence bacterial communities through soil organic carbon and pH, and that pH can indirectly affect bacteria through nitrogen content [N3-F2]. While this is soil-focused, it supports the idea that salinity-induced changes in carbon, nitrogen, and microbial interactions can alter microbial metabolism and, by extension, electron transfer in MFCs.

## How community composition changes across low, moderate, and high salinity

The evidence supports a non-linear, stepwise pattern of change. At low salinity, the community may remain relatively diverse and dominated by bacteria, but even here salinity can begin to shape composition. At moderate salinity, the literature suggests that microbial diversity and abundance can decrease, while archaea may become relatively more abundant [N3-F2]. At higher salinity, the effect becomes stronger, with studies showing that increasing salinity can reduce bacterial abundance and increase archaeal abundance, shifting the community from bacteria-dominated to archaea-dominated [N3-F2].

The specific salinity range in the cited MFC study was 3.5, 7, and 15 g/L NaCl, and it found changes in current production and bacterial community dynamics [N4-R3]. This indicates that even within a relatively narrow salinity range, microbial communities reorganize. The broader ecological study further notes that salinity can shift key microbial taxa across different salinity gradients and that low-water medium-salinity soils can have the most complex archaeal community network, whereas low-water high-salinity soils can have the most complex bacterial community network [N3-F2]. This implies that community composition is not simply a linear function of salinity but can change in complex, context-dependent ways.

## Bottom line

Overall, salinity in MFCs tends to enrich salt-tolerant and halophilic microbes, reduce sensitivity of other taxa, and restructure community composition across low, moderate, and high salinity. The evidence supports a general selective model: low salinity may preserve diversity and support a broad community, moderate salinity may begin to filter out sensitive taxa, and high salinity may favor halophilic or halotolerant organisms while altering electron transfer and metabolic pathways through physiological adaptation and community reorganization [N1-R1][N1-R2][N3-F2][N4-R3][N6-R4].

# How salinity affects electricity generation in constructed wetland MFCs

In constructed wetland microbial fuel cells (CW-MFCs), salinity has a clear and often non-linear effect on electricity generation. The evidence shows that power output and voltage can initially increase with salinity, reach an optimal range, and then decline at higher levels, while wetland design factors such as electrode configuration, plant selection, and hydraulic retention time can moderate these effects [N2-F1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-R2][N5-R5].

## How power output and voltage change with increasing salinity

The most direct evidence comes from the MDPI CW-MFC study, which reports that the system’s power generation performance first increases and then decreases with rising salinity, with the best performance at 2% salinity [N2-F1]. At that optimal point, the study records an average output voltage of 617.3 ± 25.7 mV and a power density of 45.83 mW/m² [N2-F1]. This is a strong example of a non-monotonic response: low salinity may support some baseline performance, moderate salinity may improve power generation, and high salinity may begin to inhibit it.

Another study also reports that increasing salinity first improved cell voltage, with the maximum voltage under continuous operation corresponding to a salinity level that was not explicitly stated in the excerpt but clearly associated with improved voltage [N2-R3]. This corroborates the general pattern of an initial positive response to salinity. However, the same source also notes that organic removal rates are inhibited at higher salinities, showing that salinity can improve voltage while harming other treatment outcomes [N2-R3].

## Whether there are clear optimal or inhibitory salinity ranges

The evidence suggests that optimal salinity is not a single point but a range. The MDPI study explicitly states that the power generation effect is best at 2% salinity [N2-F1], which implies that this is the optimal operating point. The study also says that salinities of 1% and above have a slight inhibitory effect on organic matter treatment, indicating that above a certain level salinity begins to become inhibitory [N6-R5]. Although this inhibition is described as “slight,” it still supports the idea that there is a threshold beyond which salinity negatively affects performance [N6-R5].

The broader literature on MFCs also supports the existence of salt tolerance thresholds. The review on substrate salinity says that increasing substrate salinity is a critical factor regulating MFC performance and that studies suggest different optimal salinities [N4-R1][N4-R2]. This means that the optimal salinity range is not universal but depends on the system and the microbial community.

## How wetland design factors moderate salinity effects on performance

Wetland design plays a major role in determining how salinity affects electricity generation. The MDPI study shows that the closed-circuit CW-MFC system with planted plants performed best, with the highest COD removal rate and power density [N2-F1]. It also notes that microbial community growth is still good under salt stress, but the structure is different [N2-F1]. This implies that plant presence can enhance both pollutant removal and power generation under saline conditions.

Electrode configuration is another key design factor. The study reports that the optimal electrode distance was 10 cm when salinity was 1%, and that optimal hydraulic retention time varied depending on whether the goal was pollutant removal or power generation [N2-F1]. This means that the same system can respond differently to salinity depending on how it is physically configured.

Plant selection also matters. The study highlights that Bruguiera gymnorrhiza exhibits strong salt tolerance and can be used as a wetland plant for the CW-MFC system [N2-F1]. This supports the idea that salt-tolerant vegetation can improve system performance under saline conditions. The broader literature on constructed wetlands also indicates that combining wetlands with MFCs enhances pollutant degradation and electricity generation [N5-R3], reinforcing the design principle that wetland structure can moderate salinity effects.

## Bottom line

For constructed wetland MFCs, salinity often follows a “first up, then down” pattern: power output and voltage may improve at moderate salinities, peak around 2% salinity, and then decline at higher levels [N2-F1][N2-R3]. Optimal salinity is therefore not a single fixed value but a range that depends on the system and microbial community [N4-R1][N4-R2]. Wetland design factors such as plant selection, electrode configuration, and hydraulic retention time can strongly moderate salinity effects, helping to maintain or even improve electricity generation in saline conditions [N2-F1][N5-R2][N5-R5].

# Salt inhibition thresholds and operational boundaries for MFCs

Salt inhibition thresholds and operational limits in MFCs are not universal; they vary by system type, microbial community, and salinity management. The evidence indicates that performance can improve, plateau, or decline depending on salinity level, and that inhibition is often linked to physiological stress, reduced microbial activity, and changes in community structure [N4-R1][N4-R3][N6-R5][N3-F2].

## The salinity ranges where performance improves, plateaus, or declines

The clearest evidence is that moderate salinity can improve performance before it becomes inhibitory. The review on substrate salinity states that increasing substrate salinity is a critical factor regulating MFC performance and that studies suggest different optimal salinities [N4-R1][N4-R2]. The MDPI CW-MFC study also reports that power generation performance first increases and then decreases with salinity, with the best performance at 2% salinity [N2-F1]. This supports a general model in which performance improves at low to moderate salinities, plateaus near the optimal point, and then declines at higher salinities.

At the same time, the evidence shows that some salinity levels can become inhibitory. The MDPI study says that salinities of 1% and above have a slight inhibitory effect on organic matter treatment [N6-R5]. Although the wording is “slight,” it still indicates a threshold beyond which performance is compromised. The broader MFC literature similarly notes that increasing salinity is a critical factor regulating performance, implying that there are operational limits where salinity becomes limiting rather than beneficial [N4-R1][N4-R2].

## What salt concentrations are considered inhibitory and why

The evidence does not provide a single universal inhibitory concentration, but it does identify thresholds where performance begins to decline. The MDPI study reports that at 2% salinity, power generation is best, while at 1% salinity the inhibitory effect on organic matter treatment is already present [N6-R5][N2-F1]. This suggests that the inhibitory threshold is at least around 1% salinity, with stronger effects above that level.

The inhibition is likely caused by a combination of physiological stress and microbial community shifts. The search material repeatedly emphasizes that halophilic and halotolerant microbes are enriched under high salinity, while salt-sensitive taxa are reduced [N1-R1][N1-R2]. In MFCs, this means that inhibition at higher salinities can occur because the dominant community shifts away from species that are efficient at electron transfer and toward species that are salt-adapted but may be less efficient at generating electricity [N3-F2][N6-R4]. Salinity can also alter electron transfer and metabolic pathways, as well as community interactions, which can further reduce performance [N1-R2][N3-F2].

## How operational limits vary with microbial community and system type

Operational limits are highly context-dependent. The MFC literature indicates that optimal salinities differ across studies, so what is optimal for one system may not be optimal for another [N4-R1][N4-R2]. The CW-MFC evidence is especially informative: the same study found that the closed-circuit system with planted plants had the best performance, and that microbial community structure changed under salt stress [N2-F1]. This means that plant selection and community composition can expand the operational window.

System type also matters. The review on plant microbial fuel cells notes that adding salt can improve performance if the system operates at an optimum level of salinity tolerance [N4-R5]. This implies that operational limits are not only biological but also engineering: a system can tolerate higher salinity if the design supports salt tolerance through electrode configuration, hydraulic retention time, and plant selection [N2-F1][N5-R2]. The broader MFC literature similarly emphasizes that substrate salinity is a critical factor, and that optimal salinities vary [N4-R1][N4-R2].

## Bottom line

Salt inhibition thresholds and operational boundaries in MFCs are not fixed. Performance can improve at low to moderate salinities, plateau near an optimal point, and then decline at higher salinities [N4-R1][N4-R2][N2-F1]. Inhibition typically begins at around 1% salinity in the cited CW-MFC study, but the exact threshold depends on the system and microbial community [N6-R5][N2-F1]. Operational limits vary with microbial community composition, electrode design, plant selection, and hydraulic configuration, meaning that the same salinity can have very different effects depending on the MFC setup [N3-F2][N2-F1][N5-R2][N4-R5].

# Tradeoffs and practical implications of salinity in MFC operation

Salinity in constructed wetland microbial fuel cells (CW-MFCs) is a double-edged sword: it can improve electricity generation at moderate salinities, but it can also harm performance at higher levels by stressing microbes and altering community structure. The practical implications are therefore about balancing salt tolerance, design optimization, and long-term system stability [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-R1][N6-R5].

## Where salinity benefits versus harms electricity generation

Salinity tends to benefit electricity generation at low to moderate levels, where the evidence shows a first-increase-then-decrease pattern. The MDPI CW-MFC study reports that power generation performance first increases and then decreases with salinity, with the best performance at 2% salinity [N2-F1]. At 2% salinity, the system produced an average output voltage of 617.3 ± 25.7 mV and a power density of 45.83 mW/m² [N2-F1]. This indicates that moderate salinity can enhance performance by favoring salt-tolerant microbes and possibly improving electron transfer efficiency [N1-R1][N1-R2].

However, salinity can also harm electricity generation at higher levels. The same study notes that salinities of 1% and above have a slight inhibitory effect on organic matter treatment [N6-R5], and that organic removal rates are inhibited with increasing salinity [N2-R3]. This means that while moderate salinity can improve power output, higher salinity can start to compromise both treatment and electricity generation [N2-F1][N2-R3].

## What operational adjustments can mitigate salinity stress

The evidence supports several practical adjustments to reduce salinity stress and improve performance. First, plant selection is important: Bruguiera gymnorrhiza, a salt-tolerant wetland plant, was used in the CW-MFC study and contributed to better performance [N2-F1]. This suggests that choosing salt-tolerant vegetation can help the system withstand saline conditions.

Second, electrode configuration matters. The study reports that the closed-circuit CW-MFC system with planted plants performed best, and that the optimal electrode distance was 10 cm when salinity was 1% [N2-F1]. It also found that the optimal hydraulic retention time varied depending on whether the goal was pollutant removal or power generation [N2-F1]. This implies that adjusting electrode spacing and hydraulic conditions can help optimize performance under saline conditions.

Third, microbial community management is relevant. The evidence shows that microbial communities reorganize under salt stress, with salt-tolerant and halophilic taxa becoming enriched while salt-sensitive taxa decline [N1-R1][N1-R2][N3-F2]. Since MFC performance depends on community composition, maintaining a community that includes salt-adapted microbes may be more effective than relying on generalist microbes under saline conditions [N3-F2].

Fourth, operational thresholds should be carefully managed. The broader MFC literature indicates that optimal salinities differ across studies, and that increasing salinity is a critical factor regulating performance [N4-R1][N4-R2]. This means that the same system can tolerate different salinities depending on microbial community and design, so operational limits should not be assumed universal [N4-R1][N4-R2].

## How salinity affects long-term stability and scalability

Salinity can affect long-term stability and scalability in two ways. On the positive side, salt-tolerant communities can persist and even thrive under saline conditions, which may improve long-term operation [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The microbial ecology study notes that soil salinity can dramatically alter diversity, composition, and interactions within microbial communities, with archaea becoming relatively more abundant while bacterial abundance may decrease [N3-F2]. This suggests that stable, salt-adapted communities may be more resilient over time.

On the negative side, salinity can reduce long-term stability if it disrupts microbial function and community structure. The evidence shows that salinity can inhibit organic removal and reduce performance at higher levels [N2-R3][N6-R5], which can make the system less reliable over time. In CW-MFCs, this matters because performance is not only determined by immediate power output but also by consistent pollutant removal and microbial community health [N2-F1][N3-F2].

Scalability is also influenced by design flexibility. The study found that the closed-circuit system with planted plants outperformed the system without planted plants [N2-F1]. This implies that scalable MFC designs should incorporate salt-tolerant plants, optimized electrode spacing, and appropriate hydraulic retention time rather than relying solely on a single configuration [N2-F1][N5-R2]. The broader MFC literature also emphasizes that optimal salinities vary, so scalable systems must be adaptable to local salinity conditions [N4-R1][N4-R2].

## Bottom line

In CW-MFCs, salinity can benefit electricity generation at moderate levels, particularly around 2% salinity, but it can also harm performance at higher salinities by stressing microbes and reducing organic removal [N2-F1][N2-R3][N6-R5]. Operational adjustments such as salt-tolerant plants, optimized electrode spacing, hydraulic retention time, and community management can mitigate salinity stress [N2-F1][N5-R2][N3-F2]. Long-term stability and scalability depend on maintaining salt-adapted communities while avoiding inhibitory salinity thresholds, making salinity management a core operational challenge [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-R1][N4-R2][N3-F2].

The microbial activity evidence shows that halophilic and halotolerant microbes become enriched, while salt-sensitive taxa decline, and that community composition shifts across low, moderate, and high salinity [N1-R1][N1-R2][N3-F2]. The operational implications are clear: plant selection, electrode configuration, hydraulic retention time, and microbial community management can all help mitigate salinity stress [N2-F1][N5-R2][N3-F2]. Long-term stability and scalability depend on balancing salt tolerance with system design and local salinity conditions [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-R1][N4-R2][N3-F2].

In short, the optimal strategy for CW-MFCs is not to avoid salinity entirely, but to operate within a narrow salinity window that favors salt-tolerant microbes while keeping salinity below inhibitory thresholds [N2-F1][N4-R1][N6-R5].

# How salinity affects microbial activity and community structure in MFCs

Salinity exerts a strong selective pressure on microbial communities in microbial fuel cells (MFCs), shifting which groups are sensitive, enriched, and structurally dominant across low, moderate, and high salinity. The evidence points to a general pattern: salt-tolerant or halophilic microbes gain prominence, while salt-sensitive taxa decline, and community composition changes in ways that can include shifts in archaeal and bacterial dominance, altered relative abundances, and changes in functional interactions [N3-F2][N4-R3][N6-R4].

## Which microbial groups are sensitive or enriched at different salinities

The strongest direct evidence is that halophilic and halotolerant microbes are specifically selected under saline conditions. The literature explicitly states that halophilic bacteria “have evolved strategies to survive in high saline concentrations” and that halotolerant and halophilic microorganisms “possess specific salt tolerance mechanisms” that make them promising in high-salt environments [N1-R1][N1-R2]. This is consistent with the broader idea that saline stress filters communities to favor salt-tolerant or halophilic taxa over salt-sensitive ones [N3-F2].

The evidence also shows that microbial community dynamics can change sharply with salinity. A study examining three salinity levels (3.5, 7, and 15 g/L NaCl) found that current production, organic removal rates, and bacterial community dynamics were all affected, indicating that microbial activity is not only reduced or enhanced depending on salinity but also reorganized [N4-R3]. Another broader microbial ecology study reports that soil salinity can dramatically alter diversity, composition, and interactions within microbial communities, with archaea becoming relatively more abundant while bacterial abundance may decrease, and that some key microbial taxa differ across salinity gradients [N3-F2]. Although this is not an MFC study, it provides a useful conceptual framework for interpreting MFC community shifts.

## How salinity alters electron transfer and metabolic pathways

The evidence is somewhat indirect, but it is clear that salinity changes microbial physiology in ways that affect electron transfer. The search material emphasizes that halophilic bacteria are remarkable for their ability to survive high salinity and that salt-tolerant microbes can have promising bioactivity under high-salt conditions [N1-R1][N1-R2]. In MFCs, this implies that electron transfer may be supported by taxa with salt-adapted metabolic pathways, rather than by generalist microbes that are inhibited at higher salinities.

The microbial ecology study also suggests that salinity can alter microbial interactions, including shifts in co-occurrence networks and keystone taxa, which can indirectly affect electron transfer by changing the functional connectivity of the community [N3-F2]. It also notes that salinity can indirectly influence bacterial communities through soil organic carbon and pH, and that pH can indirectly affect bacteria through nitrogen content [N3-F2]. While this is soil-focused, it supports the idea that salinity-induced changes in carbon, nitrogen, and microbial interactions can alter microbial metabolism and, by extension, electron transfer in MFCs.

## How community composition changes across low, moderate, and high salinity

The evidence supports a non-linear, stepwise pattern of change. At low salinity, the community may remain relatively diverse and dominated by bacteria, but even here salinity can begin to shape composition. At moderate salinity, the literature suggests that microbial diversity and abundance can decrease, while archaea may become relatively more abundant [N3-F2]. At higher salinity, the effect becomes stronger, with studies showing that increasing salinity can reduce bacterial abundance and increase archaeal abundance, shifting the community from bacteria-dominated to archaea-dominated [N3-F2].

The specific salinity range in the cited MFC study was 3.5, 7, and 15 g/L NaCl, and it found changes in current production and bacterial community dynamics [N4-R3]. This indicates that even within a relatively narrow salinity range, microbial communities reorganize. The broader ecological study further notes that salinity can shift key microbial taxa across different salinity gradients and that low-water medium-salinity soils can have the most complex archaeal community network, whereas low-water high-salinity soils can have the most complex bacterial community network [N3-F2]. This implies that community composition is not simply a linear function of salinity but can change in complex, context-dependent ways.

## Bottom line

Overall, salinity in MFCs tends to enrich salt-tolerant and halophilic microbes, reduce sensitivity of other taxa, and restructure community composition across low, moderate, and high salinity. The evidence supports a general selective model: low salinity may preserve diversity and support a broad community, moderate salinity may begin to filter out sensitive taxa, and high salinity may favor halophilic or halotolerant organisms while altering electron transfer and metabolic pathways through physiological adaptation and community reorganization [N1-R1][N1-R2][N3-F2][N4-R3][N6-R4].

# How salinity affects electricity generation in constructed wetland MFCs

In constructed wetland microbial fuel cells (CW-MFCs), salinity has a clear and often non-linear effect on electricity generation. The evidence shows that power output and voltage can initially increase with salinity, reach an optimal range, and then decline at higher levels, while wetland design factors such as electrode configuration, plant selection, and hydraulic retention time can moderate these effects [N2-F1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-R2][N5-R5].

## How power output and voltage change with increasing salinity

The most direct evidence comes from the MDPI CW-MFC study, which reports that the system’s power generation performance first increases and then decreases with rising salinity, with the best performance at 2% salinity [N2-F1]. At that optimal point, the study records an average output voltage of 617.3 ± 25.7 mV and a power density of 45.83 mW/m² [N2-F1]. This is a strong example of a non-monotonic response: low salinity may support some baseline performance, moderate salinity may improve power generation, and high salinity may begin to inhibit it.

Another study also reports that increasing salinity first improved cell voltage, with the maximum voltage under continuous operation corresponding to a salinity level that was not explicitly stated in the excerpt but clearly associated with improved voltage [N2-R3]. This corroborates the general pattern of an initial positive response to salinity. However, the same source also notes that organic removal rates are inhibited at higher salinities, showing that salinity can improve voltage while harming other treatment outcomes [N2-R3].

## Whether there are clear optimal or inhibitory salinity ranges

The evidence suggests that optimal salinity is not a single point but a range. The MDPI study explicitly states that the power generation effect is best at 2% salinity [N2-F1], which implies that this is the optimal operating point. The study also says that salinities of 1% and above have a slight inhibitory effect on organic matter treatment, indicating that above a certain level salinity begins to become inhibitory [N6-R5]. Although this inhibition is described as “slight,” it still supports the idea that there is a threshold beyond which salinity negatively affects performance [N6-R5].

The broader literature on MFCs also supports the existence of salt tolerance thresholds. The review on substrate salinity says that increasing substrate salinity is a critical factor regulating MFC performance and that studies suggest different optimal salinities [N4-R1][N4-R2]. This means that the optimal salinity range is not universal but depends on the system and the microbial community.

## How wetland design factors moderate salinity effects on performance

Wetland design plays a major role in determining how salinity affects electricity generation. The MDPI study shows that the closed-circuit CW-MFC system with planted plants performed best, with the highest COD removal rate and power density [N2-F1]. It also notes that microbial community growth is still good under salt stress, but the structure is different [N2-F1]. This implies that plant presence can enhance both pollutant removal and power generation under saline conditions.

Electrode configuration is another key design factor. The study reports that the optimal electrode distance was 10 cm when salinity was 1%, and that optimal hydraulic retention time varied depending on whether the goal was pollutant removal or power generation [N2-F1]. This means that the same system can respond differently to salinity depending on how it is physically configured.

Plant selection also matters. The study highlights that Bruguiera gymnorrhiza exhibits strong salt tolerance and can be used as a wetland plant for the CW-MFC system [N2-F1]. This supports the idea that salt-tolerant vegetation can improve system performance under saline conditions. The broader literature on constructed wetlands also indicates that combining wetlands with MFCs enhances pollutant degradation and electricity generation [N5-R3], reinforcing the design principle that wetland structure can moderate salinity effects.

## Bottom line

For constructed wetland MFCs, salinity often follows a “first up, then down” pattern: power output and voltage may improve at moderate salinities, peak around 2% salinity, and then decline at higher levels [N2-F1][N2-R3]. Optimal salinity is therefore not a single fixed value but a range that depends on the system and microbial community [N4-R1][N4-R2]. Wetland design factors such as plant selection, electrode configuration, and hydraulic retention time can strongly moderate salinity effects, helping to maintain or even improve electricity generation in saline conditions [N2-F1][N5-R2][N5-R5].

# Salt inhibition thresholds and operational boundaries for MFCs

Salt inhibition thresholds and operational limits in MFCs are not universal; they vary by system type, microbial community, and salinity management. The evidence indicates that performance can improve, plateau, or decline depending on salinity level, and that inhibition is often linked to physiological stress, reduced microbial activity, and changes in community structure [N4-R1][N4-R3][N6-R5][N3-F2].

## The salinity ranges where performance improves, plateaus, or declines

The clearest evidence is that moderate salinity can improve performance before it becomes inhibitory. The review on substrate salinity states that increasing substrate salinity is a critical factor regulating MFC performance and that studies suggest different optimal salinities [N4-R1][N4-R2]. The MDPI CW-MFC study also reports that power generation performance first increases and then decreases with salinity, with the best performance at 2% salinity [N2-F1]. This supports a general model in which performance improves at low to moderate salinities, plateaus near the optimal point, and then declines at higher salinities.

At the same time, the evidence shows that some salinity levels can become inhibitory. The MDPI study says that salinities of 1% and above have a slight inhibitory effect on organic matter treatment [N6-R5]. Although the wording is “slight,” it still indicates a threshold beyond which performance is compromised. The broader MFC literature similarly notes that increasing salinity is a critical factor regulating performance, implying that there are operational limits where salinity becomes limiting rather than beneficial [N4-R1][N4-R2].

## What salt concentrations are considered inhibitory and why

The evidence does not provide a single universal inhibitory concentration, but it does identify thresholds where performance begins to decline. The MDPI study reports that at 2% salinity, power generation is best, while at 1% salinity the inhibitory effect on organic matter treatment is already present [N6-R5][N2-F1]. This suggests that the inhibitory threshold is at least around 1% salinity, with stronger effects above that level.

The inhibition is likely caused by a combination of physiological stress and microbial community shifts. The search material repeatedly emphasizes that halophilic and halotolerant microbes are enriched under high salinity, while salt-sensitive taxa are reduced [N1-R1][N1-R2]. In MFCs, this means that inhibition at higher salinities can occur because the dominant community shifts away from species that are efficient at electron transfer and toward species that are salt-adapted but may be less efficient at generating electricity [N3-F2][N6-R4]. Salinity can also alter electron transfer and metabolic pathways, as well as community interactions, which can further reduce performance [N1-R2][N3-F2].

## How operational limits vary with microbial community and system type

Operational limits are highly context-dependent. The MFC literature indicates that optimal salinities differ across studies, so what is optimal for one system may not be optimal for another [N4-R1][N4-R2]. The CW-MFC evidence is especially informative: the same study found that the closed-circuit system with planted plants had the best performance, and that microbial community structure changed under salt stress [N2-F1]. This means that plant selection and community composition can expand the operational window.

System type also matters. The review on plant microbial fuel cells notes that adding salt can improve performance if the system operates at an optimum level of salinity tolerance [N4-R5]. This implies that operational limits are not only biological but also engineering: a system can tolerate higher salinity if the design supports salt tolerance through electrode configuration, hydraulic retention time, and plant selection [N2-F1][N5-R2]. The broader MFC literature similarly emphasizes that substrate salinity is a critical factor, and that optimal salinities vary [N4-R1][N4-R2].

## Bottom line

Salt inhibition thresholds and operational boundaries in MFCs are not fixed. Performance can improve at low to moderate salinities, plateau near an optimal point, and then decline at higher salinities [N4-R1][N4-R2][N2-F1]. Inhibition typically begins at around 1% salinity in the cited CW-MFC study, but the exact threshold depends on the system and microbial community [N6-R5][N2-F1]. Operational limits vary with microbial community composition, electrode design, plant selection, and hydraulic configuration, meaning that the same salinity can have very different effects depending on the MFC setup [N3-F2][N2-F1][N5-R2][N4-R5].

# Tradeoffs and practical implications of salinity in MFC operation

Salinity in constructed wetland microbial fuel cells (CW-MFCs) is a double-edged sword: it can improve electricity generation at moderate salinities, but it can also harm performance at higher levels by stressing microbes and altering community structure. The practical implications are therefore about balancing salt tolerance, design optimization, and long-term system stability [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-R1][N6-R5].

## Where salinity benefits versus harms electricity generation

Salinity tends to benefit electricity generation at low to moderate levels, where the evidence shows a first-increase-then-decrease pattern. The MDPI CW-MFC study reports that power generation performance first increases and then decreases with salinity, with the best performance at 2% salinity [N2-F1]. At 2% salinity, the system produced an average output voltage of 617.3 ± 25.7 mV and a power density of 45.83 mW/m² [N2-F1]. This indicates that moderate salinity can enhance performance by favoring salt-tolerant microbes and possibly improving electron transfer efficiency [N1-R1][N1-R2].

However, salinity can also harm electricity generation at higher levels. The same study notes that salinities of 1% and above have a slight inhibitory effect on organic matter treatment [N6-R5], and that organic removal rates are inhibited with increasing salinity [N2-R3]. This means that while moderate salinity can improve power output, higher salinity can start to compromise both treatment and electricity generation [N2-F1][N2-R3].

## What operational adjustments can mitigate salinity stress

The evidence supports several practical adjustments to reduce salinity stress and improve performance. First, plant selection is important: Bruguiera gymnorrhiza, a salt-tolerant wetland plant, was used in the CW-MFC study and contributed to better performance [N2-F1]. This suggests that choosing salt-tolerant vegetation can help the system withstand saline conditions.

Second, electrode configuration matters. The study reports that the closed-circuit CW-MFC system with planted plants performed best, and that the optimal electrode distance was 10 cm when salinity was 1% [N2-F1]. It also found that the optimal hydraulic retention time varied depending on whether the goal was pollutant removal or power generation [N2-F1]. This implies that adjusting electrode spacing and hydraulic conditions can help optimize performance under saline conditions.

Third, microbial community management is relevant. The evidence shows that microbial communities reorganize under salt stress, with salt-tolerant and halophilic taxa becoming enriched while salt-sensitive taxa decline [N1-R1][N1-R2][N3-F2]. Since MFC performance depends on community composition, maintaining a community that includes salt-adapted microbes may be more effective than relying on generalist microbes under saline conditions [N3-F2].

Fourth, operational thresholds should be carefully managed. The broader MFC literature indicates that optimal salinities differ across studies, and that increasing salinity is a critical factor regulating performance [N4-R1][N4-R2]. This means that the same system can tolerate different salinities depending on microbial community and design, so operational limits should not be assumed universal [N4-R1][N4-R2].

## How salinity affects long-term stability and scalability

Salinity can affect long-term stability and scalability in two ways. On the positive side, salt-tolerant communities can persist and even thrive under saline conditions, which may improve long-term operation [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The microbial ecology study notes that soil salinity can dramatically alter diversity, composition, and interactions within microbial communities, with archaea becoming relatively more abundant while bacterial abundance may decrease [N3-F2]. This suggests that stable, salt-adapted communities may be more resilient over time.

On the negative side, salinity can reduce long-term stability if it disrupts microbial function and community structure. # How salinity affects microbial activity and community structure in MFCs

Salinity exerts a strong selective pressure on microbial communities in microbial fuel cells (MFCs), shifting which groups are sensitive, enriched, and structurally dominant across low, moderate, and high salinity. The evidence points to a general pattern: salt-tolerant or halophilic microbes gain prominence, while salt-sensitive taxa decline, and community composition changes in ways that can include shifts in archaeal and bacterial dominance, altered relative abundances, and changes in functional interactions [N3-F2][N4-R3][N6-R4].

## Which microbial groups are sensitive or enriched at different salinities

The strongest direct evidence is that halophilic and halotolerant microbes are specifically selected under saline conditions. The literature explicitly states that halophilic bacteria “have evolved strategies to survive in high saline concentrations” and that halotolerant and halophilic microorganisms “possess specific salt tolerance mechanisms” that make them promising in high-salt environments [N1-R1][N1-R2]. This is consistent with the broader idea that saline stress filters communities to favor salt-tolerant or halophilic taxa over salt-sensitive ones [N3-F2].

The evidence also shows that microbial community dynamics can change sharply with salinity. A study examining three salinity levels (3.5, 7, and 15 g/L NaCl) found that current production, organic removal rates, and bacterial community dynamics were all affected, indicating that microbial activity is not only reduced or enhanced depending on salinity but also reorganized [N4-R3]. Another broader microbial ecology study reports that soil salinity can dramatically alter diversity, composition, and interactions within microbial communities, with archaea becoming relatively more abundant while bacterial abundance may decrease, and that some key microbial taxa differ across salinity gradients [N3-F2]. Although this is not an MFC study, it provides a useful conceptual framework for interpreting MFC community shifts.

## How salinity alters electron transfer and metabolic pathways

The evidence is somewhat indirect, but it is clear that salinity changes microbial physiology in ways that affect electron transfer. The search material emphasizes that halophilic bacteria are remarkable for their ability to survive high salinity and that salt-tolerant microbes can have promising bioactivity under high-salt conditions [N1-R1][N1-R2]. In MFCs, this implies that electron transfer may be supported by taxa with salt-adapted metabolic pathways, rather than by generalist microbes that are inhibited at higher salinities.

The microbial ecology study also suggests that salinity can alter microbial interactions, including shifts in co-occurrence networks and keystone taxa, which can indirectly affect electron transfer by changing the functional connectivity of the community [N3-F2]. It also notes that salinity can indirectly influence bacterial communities through soil organic carbon and pH, and that pH can indirectly affect bacteria through nitrogen content [N3-F2]. While this is soil-focused, it supports the idea that salinity-induced changes in carbon, nitrogen, and microbial interactions can alter microbial metabolism and, by extension, electron transfer in MFCs.

## How community composition changes across low, moderate, and high salinity

The evidence supports a non-linear, stepwise pattern of change. At low salinity, the community may remain relatively diverse and dominated by bacteria, but even here salinity can begin to shape composition. At moderate salinity, the literature suggests that microbial diversity and abundance can decrease, while archaea may become relatively more abundant [N3-F2]. At higher salinity, the effect becomes stronger, with studies showing that increasing salinity can reduce bacterial abundance and increase archaeal abundance, shifting the community from bacteria-dominated to archaea-dominated [N3-F2].

The specific salinity range in the cited MFC study was 3.5, 7, and 15 g/L NaCl, and it found changes in current production and bacterial community dynamics [N4-R3]. This indicates that even within a relatively narrow salinity range, microbial communities reorganize. The broader ecological study further notes that salinity can shift key microbial taxa across different salinity gradients and that low-water medium-salinity soils can have the most complex archaeal community network, whereas low-water high-salinity soils can have the most complex bacterial community network [N3-F2]. This implies that community composition is not simply a linear function of salinity but can change in complex, context-dependent ways.

## Bottom line

Overall, salinity in MFCs tends to enrich salt-tolerant and halophilic microbes, reduce sensitivity of other taxa, and restructure community composition across low, moderate, and high salinity. The evidence supports a general selective model: low salinity may preserve diversity and support a broad community, moderate salinity may begin to filter out sensitive taxa, and high salinity may favor halophilic or halotolerant organisms while altering electron transfer and metabolic pathways through physiological adaptation and community reorganization [N1-R1][N1-R2][N3-F2][N4-R3][N6-R4].

In constructed wetland microbial fuel cells (CW-MFCs), salinity has a clear and often non-linear effect on electricity generation. At that optimal point, the study records an average output voltage of 617.3 ± 25.7 mV and a power density of 45.83 mW/m² [N2-F1]. This is a strong example of a non-monotonic response: low salinity may support some baseline performance, moderate salinity may improve power generation, and high salinity may begin to inhibit it.

Another study also reports that increasing salinity first improved cell voltage, with the maximum voltage under continuous operation corresponding to a salinity level that was not explicitly stated in the excerpt but clearly associated with improved voltage [N2-R3]. This corroborates the general pattern of an initial positive response to salinity. However, the same source also notes that organic removal rates are inhibited at higher salinities, showing that salinity can improve voltage while harming other treatment outcomes [N2-R3].

## Whether there are clear optimal or inhibitory salinity ranges

The evidence suggests that optimal salinity is not a single point but a range. The MDPI study explicitly states that the power generation effect is best at 2% salinity [N2-F1], which implies that this is the optimal operating point. The study also says that salinities of 1% and above have a slight inhibitory effect on organic matter treatment, indicating that above a certain level salinity begins to become inhibitory [N6-R5]. Although this inhibition is described as “slight,” it still supports the idea that there is a threshold beyond which salinity negatively affects performance [N6-R5].

The broader literature on MFCs also supports the existence of salt tolerance thresholds. The broader literature on constructed wetlands also indicates that combining wetlands with MFCs enhances pollutant degradation and electricity generation [N5-R3], reinforcing the design principle that wetland structure can moderate salinity effects.

For constructed wetland MFCs, salinity often follows a “first up, then down” pattern: power output and voltage may improve at moderate salinities, peak around 2% salinity, and then decline at higher levels [N2-F1][N2-R3]. Optimal salinity is therefore not a single fixed value but a range that depends on the system and microbial community [N4-R1][N4-R2]. Wetland design factors such as plant selection, electrode configuration, and hydraulic retention time can strongly moderate salinity effects, helping to maintain or even improve electricity generation in saline conditions [N2-F1][N5-R2][N5-R5].

# Tradeoffs and practical implications of salinity in MFC operation

Salinity in constructed wetland microbial fuel cells (CW-MFCs) is a double-edged sword: it can improve electricity generation at moderate salinities, but it can also harm performance at higher levels by stressing microbes and altering community structure. The practical implications are therefore about balancing salt tolerance, design optimization, and long-term system stability [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-R1][N6-R5].

At 2% salinity, the system produced an average output voltage of 617.3 ± 25.7 mV and a power density of 45.83 mW/m² [N2-F1]. However, salinity can also harm electricity generation at higher levels. The same study notes that salinities of 1% and above have a slight inhibitory effect on organic matter treatment [N6-R5], and that organic removal rates are inhibited with increasing salinity [N2-R3]. This means that while moderate salinity can improve power output, higher salinity can start to compromise both treatment and electricity generation [N2-F1][N2-R3].

## What operational adjustments can mitigate salinity stress

The evidence supports several practical adjustments to reduce salinity stress and improve performance. First, plant selection is important: Bruguiera gymnorrhiza, a salt-tolerant wetland plant, was used in the CW-MFC study and contributed to better performance [N2-F1]. This suggests that choosing salt-tolerant vegetation can help the system withstand saline conditions.

Second, electrode configuration matters. The study reports that the closed-circuit CW-MFC system with planted plants performed best, and that the optimal electrode distance was 10 cm when salinity was 1% [N2-F1]. It also found that the optimal hydraulic retention time varied depending on whether the goal was pollutant removal or power generation [N2-F1]. This implies that adjusting electrode spacing and hydraulic conditions can help optimize performance under saline conditions.

Third, microbial community management is relevant. The evidence shows that microbial communities reorganize under salt stress, with salt-tolerant and halophilic taxa becoming enriched while salt-sensitive taxa decline [N1-R1][N1-R2][N3-F2]. Since MFC performance depends on community composition, maintaining a community that includes salt-adapted microbes may be more effective than relying on generalist microbes under saline conditions [N3-F2].

Fourth, operational thresholds should be carefully managed. The broader MFC literature indicates that optimal salinities differ across studies, and that increasing salinity is a critical factor regulating performance [N4-R1][N4-R2]. This means that the same system can tolerate different salinities depending on microbial community and design, so operational limits should not be assumed universal [N4-R1][N4-R2].

## How salinity affects long-term stability and scalability

Salinity can affect long-term stability and scalability in two ways. On the positive side, salt-tolerant communities can persist and even thrive under saline conditions, which may improve long-term operation [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The microbial ecology study notes that soil salinity can dramatically alter diversity, composition, and interactions within microbial communities, with archaea becoming relatively more abundant while bacterial abundance may decrease [N3-F2]. This suggests that stable, salt-adapted communities may be more resilient over time.

On the negative side, salinity can reduce long-term stability if it disrupts microbial function and community structure. The evidence shows that salinity can inhibit organic removal and reduce performance at higher levels [N2-R3][N6-R5], which can make the system less reliable over time. This implies that scalable MFC designs should incorporate salt-tolerant plants, optimized electrode spacing, and appropriate hydraulic retention time rather than relying solely on a single configuration [N2-F1][N5-R2]. The broader MFC literature also emphasizes that optimal salinities vary, so scalable systems must be adaptable to local salinity conditions [N4-R1][N4-R2].

In CW-MFCs, salinity can benefit electricity generation at moderate levels, particularly around 2% salinity, but it can also harm performance at higher salinities by stressing microbes and reducing organic removal [N2-F1][N2-R3][N6-R5]. # Integrated explanation of how salinity influences electricity generation and microbial activity in constructed wetland microbial fuel cells

Salinity in constructed wetland microbial fuel cells (CW-MFCs) is a central operational variable with both benefits and costs. It can improve electricity generation at moderate salinities, but it can also inhibit performance at higher levels by altering microbial activity, community structure, and electron transfer processes. The evidence across the three branch reports supports a consistent picture: salinity selects for salt-tolerant microbes, changes community composition, and often follows a non-linear performance pattern, with optimal operation occurring in a narrow salinity window [N3-F2][N2-F1][N4-R1][N6-R5].

## 1. How salinity affects microbial activity and community structure

Salinity exerts a strong selective pressure on microbial communities in MFCs. The evidence shows that halophilic and halotolerant microbes are enriched under saline conditions, while salt-sensitive taxa are reduced [N1-R1][N1-R2]. This means that microbial activity is not uniform across salinities: salt-tolerant microbes become more prominent, and the community reorganizes around them [N3-F2].

The evidence also indicates that community composition changes in a non-linear way. At low salinity, the community may remain relatively diverse, but salinity begins to shape the relative abundance of taxa. At moderate salinity, microbial diversity and abundance can decrease, while archaea may become relatively more abundant [N3-F2]. At higher salinity, the effect becomes stronger, with studies showing that increasing salinity can reduce bacterial abundance and increase archaeal abundance, shifting the community from bacteria-dominated to archaea-dominated [N3-F2]. This supports the idea that community structure changes progressively with salinity rather than in a simple linear fashion.

Salinity also alters electron transfer and metabolic pathways. The branch reports emphasize that halophilic bacteria have evolved strategies to survive high salinity and that salt-tolerant microbes possess specific salt tolerance mechanisms [N1-R1][N1-R2]. In MFCs, this implies that electron transfer is supported by taxa with salt-adapted metabolic pathways, rather than by generalist microbes that are inhibited at higher salinities. The microbial community shift evidence also suggests that salinity can alter interactions among microbes, including changes in co-occurrence networks and keystone taxa, which can indirectly affect electron transfer by changing functional connectivity [N3-F2].

## 2. How salinity affects electricity generation in CW-MFCs

In constructed wetland MFCs, salinity has a clear and often non-linear effect on electricity generation. The evidence shows that power output and voltage can first increase with salinity, reach an optimal range, and then decline at higher levels [N2-F1][N2-R3]. The MDPI CW-MFC study reports that the system’s power generation performance first increases and then decreases with rising salinity, with the best performance at 2% salinity [N2-F1]. At that optimal point, the study records an average output voltage of 617.3 ± 25.7 mV and a power density of 45.83 mW/m² [N2-F1]. This is a strong example of the general pattern: moderate salinity can improve performance, but higher salinity can begin to inhibit it.

The evidence also shows that organic removal is harmed at higher salinities. The same study notes that salinities of 1% and above have a slight inhibitory effect on organic matter treatment, while organic removal rates are inhibited with increasing salinity [N6-R5][N2-R3]. This means that electricity generation is not the only outcome affected by salinity; treatment performance can also decline, especially at higher salinities [N2-F1][N2-R3].

## 3. Where salinity benefits versus harms electricity generation

The branch reports indicate that salinity benefits electricity generation at low to moderate levels, but harms it at higher levels. Moderate salinities appear to favor salt-tolerant communities and can improve power output and voltage [N2-F1][N2-R3]. However, higher salinities can begin to inhibit performance by stressing microbes and reducing organic removal [N6-R5][N2-R3]. The broader MFC literature supports this pattern, noting that increasing substrate salinity is a critical factor regulating MFC performance and that studies suggest different optimal salinities [N4-R1][N4-R2].

## 4. What operational adjustments can mitigate salinity stress

The evidence points to several practical adjustments that can reduce salinity stress and improve CW-MFC performance. First, plant selection matters: Bruguiera gymnorrhiza, a salt-tolerant wetland plant, was used in the CW-MFC study and contributed to better performance [N2-F1]. This suggests that choosing salt-tolerant vegetation can help the system withstand saline conditions.

Second, electrode configuration is important. The study reports that the closed-circuit CW-MFC system with planted plants performed best, and that the optimal electrode distance was 10 cm when salinity was 1% [N2-F1]. It also found that the optimal hydraulic retention time varied depending on whether the goal was pollutant removal or power generation [N2-F1]. This implies that adjusting electrode spacing and hydraulic conditions can help optimize performance under saline conditions.

Third, microbial community management is relevant. The evidence shows that microbial communities reorganize under salt stress, with salt-tolerant and halophilic taxa becoming enriched while salt-sensitive taxa decline [N1-R1][N1-R2][N3-F2]. Since MFC performance depends on community composition, maintaining a community that includes salt-adapted microbes may be more effective than relying on generalist microbes under saline conditions [N3-F2].

Fourth, operational thresholds should be carefully managed. The broader MFC literature indicates that optimal salinities differ across studies, and that increasing salinity is a critical factor regulating performance [N4-R1][N4-R2]. This means that the same system can tolerate different salinities depending on microbial community and design, so operational limits should not be assumed universal [N4-R1][N4-R2].

## 5. How salinity affects long-term stability and scalability

Salinity can affect long-term stability and scalability in two ways. On the positive side, salt-tolerant communities can persist and even thrive under saline conditions, which may improve long-term operation [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The microbial ecology study notes that soil salinity can dramatically alter diversity, composition, and interactions within microbial communities, with archaea becoming relatively more abundant while bacterial abundance may decrease [N3-F2]. This suggests that stable, salt-adapted communities may be more resilient over time.

On the negative side, salinity can reduce long-term stability if it disrupts microbial function and community structure. The evidence shows that salinity can inhibit organic removal and reduce performance at higher levels [N2-R3][N6-R5], which can make the system less reliable over time. In CW-MFCs, this matters because performance is not only determined by immediate power output but also by consistent pollutant removal and microbial community health [N2-F1][N3-F2].

Scalability is also influenced by design flexibility. The study found that the closed-circuit system with planted plants outperformed the system without planted plants [N2-F1]. This implies that scalable MFC designs should incorporate salt-tolerant plants, optimized electrode spacing, and appropriate hydraulic retention time rather than relying solely on a single configuration [N2-F1][N5-R2]. The broader MFC literature also emphasizes that optimal salinities vary, so scalable systems must be adaptable to local salinity conditions [N4-R1][N4-R2].

## 6. Integrated conclusion

Overall, salinity in constructed wetland MFCs is a double-edged sword: it can improve electricity generation at moderate salinities, especially around 2% salinity, but it can also inhibit performance at higher levels by stressing microbes and reducing organic removal [N2-F1][N2-R3][N6-R5]. The microbial activity evidence shows that halophilic and halotolerant microbes become enriched, while salt-sensitive taxa decline, and that community composition shifts across low, moderate, and high salinity [N1-R1][N1-R2][N3-F2]. The operational implications are clear: plant selection, electrode configuration, hydraulic retention time, and microbial community management can all help mitigate salinity stress [N2-F1][N5-R2][N3-F2]. Long-term stability and scalability depend on balancing salt tolerance with system design and local salinity conditions [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-R1][N4-R2][N3-F2].

In short, the optimal strategy for CW-MFCs is not to avoid salinity entirely, but to operate within a narrow salinity window that favors salt-tolerant microbes while keeping salinity below inhibitory thresholds [N2-F1][N4-R1][N6-R5].
